fields.expected: Most of my recent work has been on LLM and agent systems where the hard part is reliability, not generation. In my job-application agent I used Playwright for browser control with OpenAI called only at narrow, well-defined sites, Zod for schema validation, and SQLite as the single source of truth, because agent state diverging across processes is how you end up submitting a real application by accident. Free-text and demographic fields are architecturally blocked from autofill and always route to human review. In tSearch I built a rubric-driven LLM judging system where separate judges score dimensions in parallel and then synthesize an evidence-cited assessment, with discovery kept separate from assessment so judges cannot silently paper over identity-resolution errors. At SAC Nexus I work on temporal sequence modeling over event streams with RNN and Transformer-style approaches, a learning-to-rank layer for alert prioritization, and a retrieval-augmented explanation layer served through a versioned FastAPI microservice. I have also trained CNNs in PyTorch, gradient-boosted models with XGBoost plus SHAP interpretation, and built retrieval with OpenAI embeddings, Pinecone, and Neo4j. At Intelehealth I designed an evaluation framework comparing model outputs against a 4,169-case clinical standard.

fields.expected: Notion describes itself as a workspace where teams and agents think together, and that framing is close to the problem I have spent the last year building around: where machine action should stop and human judgment should take over. I built a Playwright job-application agent in TypeScript where every application moves through an explicit state machine, SQLite is the single source of truth because browser state diverging across processes is how automation quietly does the wrong thing, and mutating capabilities sit behind fail-closed flags that never default on. Free-text essays and demographic fields are architecturally prevented from being auto-filled and always generate a human-review item. I did that because I do not think more autonomy is automatically better, especially in a product people rely on daily. Agents inside a workspace have the same property: a wrong action is not an abstract eval failure, it is someone's document or workflow. I also care about shipping things people actually use, which is why the Hopkins pilot for ClarityAtlas with 30+ users mattered more to me than the model work behind it. I would want to work on the agent and evaluation side here.
